query: High-entropy alloys contain five or more elements at 5–35 at% each, generally with comparable atomic radii. Refractory and nickel-based high-entropy alloys have demonstrated elevated-temperature mechanical properties comparable to titanium- and nickel-based alloys used in extreme environments because of their heat resistance and specific strength. However, prior investigations have mainly treated titanium and nickel as additions, leaving alloys in which both are primary constituents unexplored. Subject to the stated compositional definition, what single testable intervention hypothesis could improve the elevated-temperature mechanical properties of a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy relative to the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted relative outcome, composition and operating boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding 1–3 at% tungsten to a titanium‐ and nickel‐primary high-entropy alloy will enhance its elevated-temperature mechanical properties relative to the same alloy without tungsten by promoting solid-solution strengthening and impeding dislocation motion.
generation.material_initial_state: A titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy containing at least five elements each within 5–35 at% with comparable atomic radii, without tungsten.
generation.intervention: Introduce 1–3 at% tungsten into the alloy composition while maintaining the high-entropy criteria.
generation.conditions: Mechanical testing at elevated temperatures, for example within the 700–900°C range, under typical tensile and creep testing conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced lattice distortion and possible formation of tungsten-related microstructural features (e.g., fine tungsten-rich regions) that impede dislocation motion.
generation.mechanism: The tungsten addition increases lattice distortion, thereby creating a more effective barrier to dislocation movement and grain boundary sliding, which improves yield strength and creep resistance at high temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: The tungsten-modified alloy is expected to exhibit higher yield strength and reduced creep rates at elevated temperatures compared to the baseline alloy without tungsten.
generation.baseline: A titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy processed under identical conditions but without tungsten addition.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to high-entropy alloys with primary constituents titanium and nickel (and at least three additional elements at 5–35 at% each) with tungsten addition limited to 1–3 at%, and its effects are expected in the temperature range of approximately 700–900°C.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the detailed microstructural evolution of tungsten at the upper limit of the temperature range and the precise quantitative improvement in mechanical properties.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of high-entropy alloy samples: one group as the baseline titanium- and nickel-primary alloy without tungsten and one group with 1–3 at% tungsten added. Subject both groups to identical processing (melting, casting, heat treatment) and then perform a series of high-temperature tensile and creep tests in the 700–900°C range. Complement mechanical tests with microstructural analyses using TEM and XRD to identify tungsten-induced microstructural features.
measurements: Creep rate under constant load at elevated temperatures
Microstructural characteristics (e.g., lattice distortion, tungsten-rich precipitate formation)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the tungsten-added alloy does not demonstrate a statistically significant improvement (e.g., >10% increase in yield strength and a reduced creep rate) over the baseline alloy, or if the intended tungsten-induced microstructural modifications are not observed, the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Adding a small amount (e.g., approximately 1–3 at%) of tungsten to a titanium‐ and nickel‐primary high-entropy alloy will improve its high-temperature mechanical properties relative to the same alloy without tungsten.
drafts.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy whose principal constituents are titanium and nickel (with other elements meeting the 5–35 at% criterion) and produced without tungsten.
drafts.intervention: Introduce 1–3 at% tungsten into the alloy while keeping the overall composition within the high-entropy criteria.
drafts.conditions: Mechanical testing at elevated temperatures (e.g., 700–900°C) relevant to extreme high-temperature environments, with the alloy processed via conventional melting and heat treatment to produce a homogeneous microstructure.
drafts.structural_mediator: Formation of fine tungsten-rich precipitates or enhanced tungsten solute incorporation within the matrix, leading to microstructural features that impede dislocation motion and grain boundary sliding.
drafts.mechanism: Tungsten, as a refractory element, can promote solid-solution strengthening and/or precipitation hardening by forming nanoscale secondary phases. These features are expected to increase yield strength and retard creep deformation at elevated temperatures.
drafts.predicted_outcome: The tungsten-modified alloy will exhibit a measurably higher yield strength and improved creep resistance at elevated temperatures compared to the alloy without tungsten.
drafts.baseline: The titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy without any tungsten addition.
drafts.boundary: The alloy composition must remain within the high-entropy definition (i.e., five or more elements with 5–35 at% each) with tungsten addition limited to about 1–3 at%. Testing conditions should reflect temperatures in the range of 700–900°C where high-temperature mechanical performance is critical.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two batches of the alloy: one as the baseline titanium/nickel-primary high-entropy alloy and one with an additional 2 at% tungsten (with minor adjustments to the balance of elements to maintain overall composition criteria). Subject both alloys to identical melting, casting, and heat-treatment procedures. Perform high-temperature tensile and creep tests at, for example, 800°C. Complement mechanical tests with microstructural analysis using TEM and XRD to assess the presence and nature of tungsten-rich precipitates or solid-solution effects.
measurements: Microstructural features related to tungsten incorporation (precipitate size/distribution)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the tungsten-added alloy does not show a statistically significant improvement in yield strength and reduced creep rates at 800°C relative to the baseline or if the intended tungsten-induced microstructural modifications (e.g., tungsten-rich precipitates) are not observed, the hypothesis will be falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: If a baseline Ti20Ni20Cr20Co20Fe20 high-entropy alloy is partially substituted with ~7 at% Al and subsequently subjected to a two-step heat treatment, stable Ni3Al-based precipitates will form, strengthening the titanium- and nickel-primary alloy at elevated temperatures relative to the undoped or unaged baseline.
drafts.material_initial_state: A near-equiatomic high-entropy alloy with approximately 20 at% Ti, 20 at% Ni, 20 at% Cr, 20 at% Co, and 20 at% Fe (five principal elements at 5–35 at% each).
drafts.intervention: Introduce 7 at% Al by substituting part of the Fe content (7 at% Al, 13 at% Fe) and perform a two-step aging treatment (solution-anneal at 1100°C for 2 hours, followed by water quenching, then age at 750°C for 4 hours).
drafts.conditions: Samples tested in a high-temperature environment (600–800°C), inert or vacuum atmosphere to minimize oxidation, employing standard tensile and creep-testing protocols.
drafts.structural_mediator: Formation of Ni3Al-type nanoprecipitates within the alloy matrix that includes titanium and nickel as primary constituents.
drafts.mechanism: The precipitates serve as obstacles to dislocation motion, leading to enhanced strength and creep resistance at elevated temperatures by precipitation strengthening.
drafts.predicted_outcome: The Al-doped, aged alloy will show a >10% increase in high-temperature yield strength and improved creep resistance compared to the baseline without Al doping.
drafts.baseline: An undoped Ti20Ni20Cr20Co20Fe20 alloy processed under identical parameters but without Al substitution or the aging step.
drafts.boundary: The strengthening effect is expected to persist up to ~800°C, above which precipitate coarsening may reduce the improvement.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce and solution-anneal two alloys (baseline Ti20Ni20Cr20Co20Fe20 and Al-doped Ti20Ni20Cr20Co20Fe13Al7), then age them at 750°C for 4 hours. Subsequently, perform identical high-temperature tensile and creep tests.
measurements: Creep rate at 800°C under constant load
Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) for Ni3Al precipitate morphology
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If there is no measurable increase in yield strength or creep resistance in the Al-doped alloy at 600–800°C compared to the baseline, or there is no evidence of stable Ni3Al-type precipitates, then the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Introducing a small amount (1-2 at%) of hafnium (Hf) into a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy will improve its elevated-temperature mechanical properties by promoting solid-solution strengthening and stabilizing the microstructure at high temperatures.
drafts.material_initial_state: A titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy containing five or more elements at 5–35 at% each, with no hafnium present.
drafts.intervention: Add 1-2 at% hafnium (Hf) to the titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy.
drafts.conditions: Elevated-temperature conditions (e.g., 800–1000°C) relevant to extreme environments such as aerospace or power generation applications.
drafts.structural_mediator: Solid-solution strengthening and microstructural stabilization due to the incorporation of hafnium atoms, which have a larger atomic radius and high melting point.
drafts.mechanism: Hafnium atoms, due to their larger atomic radius, create lattice distortions that impede dislocation motion, enhancing strength. Additionally, hafnium's high melting point contributes to thermal stability, reducing grain boundary mobility and phase instability at elevated temperatures.
drafts.predicted_outcome: The titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy with 1-2 at% hafnium will exhibit higher yield strength and creep resistance at elevated temperatures compared to the same alloy without hafnium.
drafts.baseline: The mechanical properties of the titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy without hafnium under the same elevated-temperature conditions.
drafts.boundary: The hypothesis applies to titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloys with 5–35 at% of each element, tested at temperatures between 800–1000°C. The effect may diminish outside this compositional range or temperature window.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy samples: one with 1-2 at% hafnium added and one without. Subject both sets to tensile and creep tests at 800–1000°C.
measurements: Microstructural analysis (e.g., grain size, phase stability) before and after testing
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the alloy with hafnium does not show a statistically significant improvement in yield strength or creep resistance compared to the alloy without hafnium, or if microstructural analysis shows no evidence of solid-solution strengthening or thermal stabilization, the hypothesis will be falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Incorporating a small percentage of aluminum (5 at%) into a titanium-nickel high-entropy alloy will improve its elevated-temperature mechanical properties compared to the same alloy without aluminum.
drafts.intervention: Addition of 5 at% aluminum to the titanium-nickel high-entropy alloy.
drafts.structural_mediator: Formation of aluminum-rich phases that enhance the alloy's strength and ductility at high temperatures.
drafts.mechanism: The addition of aluminum is expected to stabilize the high-temperature phases and improve the alloy's resistance to deformation under stress.
drafts.predicted_outcome: The titanium-nickel-aluminum high-entropy alloy will exhibit improved yield strength and ductility at elevated temperatures compared to the titanium-nickel alloy without aluminum.
drafts.boundary: The hypothesis is limited to titanium-nickel alloys with 5 at% aluminum at elevated temperatures above 600°C.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct mechanical tests (tensile and creep tests) on both the titanium-nickel alloy and the titanium-nickel-aluminum alloy at elevated temperatures.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the titanium-nickel-aluminum alloy does not show a statistically significant improvement in yield strength or ductility compared to the titanium-nickel alloy, the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Addition of a refractory element with a larger atomic radius to a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy improves its elevated-temperature mechanical properties.
drafts.material_initial_state: Titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy with 5-35 at% of each primary constituent and comparable atomic radii.
drafts.intervention: Addition of a refractory element (e.g., tungsten or molybdenum) with a larger atomic radius to the alloy composition.
drafts.structural_mediator: Formation of a solid solution with lattice distortion and increased diffusion barrier.
drafts.mechanism: The added refractory element with a larger atomic radius increases the lattice distortion and solid solution strengthening, leading to improved high-temperature strength and creep resistance.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Improved elevated-temperature mechanical properties, including increased yield strength and creep resistance, relative to the same material without the intervention.
drafts.baseline: Titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy without the added refractory element.
drafts.boundary: Composition: 5-35 at% of each primary constituent (titanium and nickel), with the added refractory element at 1-10 at%; Temperature: 500-1000°C.

falsification_experiment.design: Compare the elevated-temperature mechanical properties of the titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy with and without the added refractory element.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the addition of the refractory element does not result in a significant improvement (e.g., >10%) in elevated-temperature mechanical properties, the hypothesis is falsified.
